newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Crime experts seek ways to keep tabs on dirty money.
newsitem.headline: Crime experts seek ways to keep tabs on dirty money.

text.p: Police, bankers and financial regulators from 32 countries met in Buenos Aires Tuesday to swap ideas on how to combat money-laundering and keep crime syndicates out of the global banking system.

"We believe an effective anti-money-laundering program will keep little crooks little and stop them from becoming big criminal organizations," the director of the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Stanley Morris, said at the opening of the two-day conference.

Experts on financial crime estimate that $500 billion of dirty money, much of it the spoils of drug smuggling and arms dealing, is laundered in the world every year, though the nature of the crime makes any estimate unreliable.
Interpol and FinCEN have gathered law enforcement agencies and financial regulators together with bankers and accountants to exchange ideas on detecting and stopping illegal money transactions.

"Private bankers have as much responsibility in identifying transactions as the police," Morris told reporters. "Organized crime uses its money and uses the financial system just as legitimate businesses do."
Argentine Interior Minister Carlos Corach, opening the conference, spoke of "cause for optimism" in the fight against money-laundering.
Morris said that even "notorious offshore banking centers" like the Cayman Islands were taking steps to "ensure their banks do not become tainted with dirty money".

"Increasingly banks around the world are recognizing that the easy acceptance of dirty money has a bad influence on the economy," Morris said. "It creates economic disruption and lets organized crime develop increased power in a country."
Fernando Carpentieri, head of the 26-nation Financial Action Task Force (FATF), said countries that failed to keep tabs on dirty money risked being controlled by criminals.
"There is the danger that once criminal money enters the financial circuit, the criminals will get control of the money circuits and eventually of production itself," he added.
The FATF was set up by the Group of Seven industrialized nations in 1989. Members evaluate each other's money-laundering controls.
At present it has no members from Latin America or Africa, and only three from Asia. "We are very much interested in expanding it," Morris said.
